newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Yen's fall erodes S.Korean exports gain.
newsitem.headline: Yen's fall erodes S.Korean exports gain.

text.p: The South Korean won's slide against the dollar ought to be good news for exporters, except that the yen is losing ground faster and Japan may end up the biggest winner, economists said on Wednesday.
Export-oriented industries were counting on the won's decline giving them an edge over their Japanese rivals as world prices for semiconductors, steel and petrochemicals plunge.
The won's softness was one of the bright spots in an otherwise bleak outlook.
But the benefits are being eroded by the yen's decline because South Korea and Japan compete in similar markets and with many of the same products.
"A weaker won gives local exporters a price edge," said Lee Chang-seon, an economist at LG Economic Research Institute. "But much of the gain is being erased by the yen's weakness."
The yen has depreciated by 9.5 percent against the dollar this year, while the won has lost 7.2 percent.
On Tuesday the won plunged to a new six-year low of 834.50 against the dollar but strengthened on Wednesday to close at 830.40.
According to a poll taken by Reuters, economists and dealers expect the local unit to weaken to the 835-840 won level by the end of the year.

"The dollar is expected to rise further to 840 won by the end of the year," said Jung In-woo, a foreign exchange dealer at Korea First Bank. "Import deals will continue to flow in. And there is an acute shortage of dollars in the market."
"Until now, concerns over the yen's depreciation have been exaggerated," said Rhee Namuh, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities. "But from now on this has to be taken seriously."

Rhee said Japanese companies had not yet cut prices in line with the yen's fall. "But if the yen slips to 120 in the next six to nine months, they are sure to cut export prices and it could hurt Korean exporters."
The yen stood at 114.27 on Wednesday.
Economists said the won's fall would make imports more expensive, offsetting any export gains since South Korean firms are heavily reliant on imported raw materials and capital goods.
"Oil refining and paper companies will be hit most by the rising dollar as they rely mostly on imports of raw materials," said Rhee of Dongbang Peregrine.

South Korea's current account deficit exploded to $17.09 billion in the first nine months of this year, more than doubling from $8.08 billion a year ago. Economists forecast a $20 billion shortfall for all of 1996.
"The dollar/yen factor will be a huge variable in determining the won's future and the economy," said Lee of LG.
